entities.name: Adolph Gregory Schmitt
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Adolph Gregory Schmitt (1884–1958) was an American Catholic bishop of the Capuchin Franciscan order who served as a missionary bishop in Japan during one of the most extraordinary periods in Japanese history. Born in Ohio, he professed as a Capuchin and was sent to Japan, where he was appointed bishop and served through World War II, the atomic bombing, and the postwar occupation.

Schmitt led a Catholic mission community in Japan through the extreme conditions of wartime, including the internment of foreign missionaries after Pearl Harbor. His survival through the war and his continued presence in Japan during the American occupation placed him in a unique position to minister to both Japanese Catholics and American servicemen. The postwar period saw a brief moment of hope for Catholic expansion in Japan as MacArthur's occupation opened the country to missionary activity.

His career represents the extraordinary personal commitment required of missionary bishops in imperial-era Japan—a country that had historically persecuted Christianity and that only gradually permitted Catholic activity. The Capuchin presence in Japan, maintained through war, occupation, and reconstruction, contributed to the small but resilient Japanese Catholic community that exists today.
